idiom_name: per-hop durable store + positive acknowledgement + replay on restart
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: split the path into hops and accept a message at each hop only by copying it into a durable store (a file followed by fsync, a database row, a broker log entry), then hand the next hop a reference to that stored copy. The next hop acknowledges after it has stored - and at the last hop processed and committed - the message; only on that acknowledgement may the previous copy be deleted. A recovery process replays anything still stored but unacknowledged, so restart is part of normal operation rather than an exception path. Deduplicate on a stable, business-derived message id or make the handler idempotent, because every failure in this protocol surfaces as a duplicate delivery. Which technology plays the store is a deployment decision: broker log, message-store table, transactional outbox, OS-persisted work queue or a hand-written spool file.
code_sketch:
send(m):
    store.put(m.id, m)                      # durable; the send is not complete before this
    try: transport.write(m); wait_for_ack()  # ack means: stored at the next hop
    except Timeout: schedule_replay(m.id)    # leave the copy in the store
    else: store.delete(m.id)                 # only now may we forget it
recovery(): for m in store.unacked(): replay(m)
receive(m): commit_business_effect(m); dedup(m.id); ack(m)
pitfalls: Treating a successful transport write as delivery; only the stored and acknowledged state counts.
Deleting from the store before the next hop confirmed - the window between write and ack is exactly where messages get lost.
Skipping deduplication or idempotence, so the first redelivery after a crash doubles the business effect.
RabbitMQ: enabling publisher confirms but never inspecting the result - nack-ed messages are silently lost on broker failure before persist.
Kafka: using idempotent producer without transactional.id for cross-session exactly-once - a producer restart assigns a new PID, breaking dedup across restarts.
AWS SQS: treating standard queues as exactly-once - they provide at-least-once only; use FIFO queues with content-based deduplication for exactly-once.
GCP Pub/Sub: enabling exactly-once on a push subscription - only pull subscriptions support the guarantee; push deliveries can still duplicate.
Azure Service Bus: using peek-lock but closing the receiver before settling - the lock expires and the message redelivers before the settlement call completes.
Setting visibility timeout shorter than processing time - another consumer claims the message while the original is still working, causing duplicate delivery.
Network partition during the window between processing completion and acknowledgement - the message is redelivered after the business effect already applied, with no idempotency guard.
DLQ payload containing sensitive data (PII, credentials) with no redaction - the dead-letter store becomes an unguarded data store subject to breach.
Unbounded retry without exponential backoff on a failing downstream dependency - retry storms amplify the outage and may trigger circuit breakers that slow recovery.

Kafka: setting min.insync.replicas=1 (the default in some bootstrap configs) combined with unclean.leader.election.enabled=true allows data loss during unclean leader failover — these two settings must be set together, not independently.

Misconfiguring the prefetch count (Kafka's max.poll.records, RabbitMQ's prefetch, SQS's receive batch) too high: a consumer crash loses an entire in-flight batch, causing a large duplicate burst on redelivery that can overwhelm downstream systems.

Using a TTL that expires messages while they are still in-flight for processing (visibility timeout > TTL): the message is deleted by the broker while the consumer is actively working on it, causing silent data loss with no redelivery signal.

Implementing a custom retry loop but forgetting to cap the total retry count, then hitting an unbounded exponential backoff that causes a retry storm — the downstream service becomes a victim of the retry traffic it is already struggling to handle.

Cloud provider regional outages overlapping with DLQ redrive: replaying a DLQ while the source queue's broker is still recovering can cause messages to be redelivered to consumers that have already moved on, creating ordering violations and late-delivery anomalies.

Wrong move: Treat RabbitMQ publisher confirms as proof that a message reached a consumer -> the broker confirmation covers broker acceptance or persistence, not the committed business effect -> instead retain a replayable copy until consumer processing commits and its acknowledgement is settled.

Wrong move: Enable Kafka idempotence and call it cross-session exactly-once -> idempotence alone does not atomically couple external state and is limited to its producer session -> instead use transactional.id with read_committed where appropriate and make the sink idempotent.

Wrong move: Select an Amazon SQS Standard queue when duplicates violate a business invariant -> Standard queues are at-least-once and FIFO deduplication is bounded by its window -> instead use FIFO within the documented window or persist a business-key idempotency record.
